analytic.title: Reliability-Aware Real-Time Task Mapping for Multi-Server Edge Computing Systems With DVFS

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Edge computing enhances user Quality of Experience (QoE) by deploying computing and storage resources at the network edge, enabling efficient management and scheduling of offloaded tasks. Application execution performance is primarily determined by task mapping. However, multi-server edge networks face challenges due to potential failures in hardware or software, where both permanent faults in devices or links and transient faults during task execution can harm task completion. Additionally, real-time responsiveness and energy efficiency are critical for service quality and system sustainability. To address these limitations, we propose a Reliability-Aware Task Mapping (RATM) method integrating task duplication, DVFS, and communication link selection to optimize energy consumption while satisfying task reliability and real-time constraints. The joint design is formulated as a complex nonlinear optimization problem and is linearized to find the optimal solution. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches regarding system energy efficiency, task reliability, and schedulability.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Recently, the rapid growth of data-intensive applications and complex service demands (e.g., autonomous driving, federated learning, and multi-agent collaboration) has made highperformance computing and energy efficiency become critical concerns in mobile and edge computing systems [1]. However, edge devices typically possess limited computational resources and energy supply. To handle complex computational tasks, Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) offloads tasks to edge servers via wireless networks, enhancing computation speed and user's Quality of Experience (QoE) [2].

In multi-server edge computing systems, the task mapping mechanism allocates tasks to suitable edge servers based on resource availability and task requirements, significantly impacting the system's energy consumption, real-time responsiveness, and reliability [3]. To enhance energy efficiency, edge servers commonly support Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS), enabling dynamic adjustment of voltage and frequency during the task execution process. However, lower Voltage/Frequency (V/F) levels reduce energy consumption but also increase execution time and transient fault rates [4]. Task duplication is typically utilized to improve reliability; however, duplicating the entire task set may increase execution and communication overhead. Allocating dependent tasks to different servers involves data transmission, where communication costs (time and energy) are non-negligible compared to computing costs [5]. In mesh networks, data transmission between source and destination switches may traverse multiple paths, and compared to traditional single-path or fixed routing (e.g., XY routing) [6], communication overhead can be further reduced by selecting proper communication links. Furthermore, permanent faults caused by hardware damage or software crashes in edge networks can lead to service failures, especially in edge nodes exposed to environmental risks [7]. Unlike transient faults, permanent faults cannot recover quickly and may cause task interruptions without fault-handling mechanisms [8]. Therefore, it is essential to selectively utilize available links and servers based on the fault status to ensure task reliability.

Compared with state-of-the-art methods, we propose a novel task mapping method for multi-server edge network systems, mitigating the impact of server, switch, and link failures through optimized task allocation and communication path selection. Additionally, by integrating DVFS and task duplication, the method reduces transient fault effects during execution, enhancing energy efficiency while meeting real-time and reliability constraints. Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• A Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) formulation for energy efficiency Reliability-Aware Task Mapping (RATM) method on multi-server edge networks with multiple constraints.

• To find the optimal solution, the original problem is equivalently converted to a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem without quality loss. • We conduct extensive simulations to evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, and the results show that our method outperforms other techniques in terms of energy efficiency and task reliability improvement. 1) Related Work: Task scheduling in edge computing has been extensively studied. Existing works focus on reducing computing energy consumption in edge systems through task mapping and DVFS [9], [10]. Lower V/F levels may increase the transient fault rate of tasks, and thus, task duplication is employed to enhance task reliability [11], [12]. Integrating DVFS with task duplication can reduce energy consumption while meeting task reliability requirements. However, existing works do not consider the above issues comprehensively. In addition, to reduce communication overhead in edge networks, some works consider the issue of path selection between the switches [13]. Nevertheless, they do not consider the potential failure of links, which leads to data transmission failures. Furthermore, few studies have investigated the impact of permanent faults in nodes or links of edge systems during task execution. To enhance task reliability, common approaches include node failure prediction or rescheduling tasks [8], [14]. However, these approaches only focus on task allocation on servers and do not consider the selection of communication links between switches in scenarios with link failures.

2) Organization: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the system model, the problem formulation, and the linearization method. Section III shows the simulation results, and Section IV concludes this work.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND PROBLEM FORMULATION
div.p: A. System Model 1) System Architecture: This paper considers an edge network consisting of edge servers, switches, and communication links between them. As shown in Fig. 1, the edge network topology could be represented by a directed graph G SY S = (S ∪ R, E E ∪ E B ), where S = {S 1 , . . . , S K } and R = {R 1 , . . . , R N } are the sets of K edge servers and N switches that handle data forwarding, respectively. E E = {e 11 , e 12 , . . . , e KN } is the set of edge communication links (denoted as edge links), where e kn represents the bidirectional connection between edge server S k and switch R n (∀k ∈ {1, . . . , K}, ∀n ∈ {1, . . . , N }). E B = {ϵ 11 , ϵ 12 , . . . , ϵ N N } is the set of core communication links (denoted as core links), where ϵ mn represents the unidirectional connection between switch R m and switch R n (∀m ̸ = n ∈ {1, . . . , N }), i.e., the data are transmitted from R m to R n through ϵ mn .

2) Task Model: We consider a dependent task set U that contains M 0 periodic real-time tasks released at the time 0 and shares a common scheduling horizon H. The dependencies among the tasks are represented by a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) G 0 = (U 0 , E 0 ), where the vertexes U 0 = {u 1 , . . . , u M0 } represent the tasks to be executed, while the edges E 0 represent the data dependencies among the tasks. Each task u i is characterized by a tuple {C i , T D i , D ij , p ij , H}, where C i and T D i denote the Worst Case Execution Cycle (WCEC) and the deadline of u i , respectively. In the dependency matrix p = [p ij ] M0×M0 , the element p ij is defined as p ij = 1 if task u i precedes task u j and u j is the immediate successor of u i ; otherwise, p ij = 0. As the task DAG shown in Fig. 1, we have p 12 = p 13 = p 24 = p 34 = 1. Based on the dependency matrix p, we derive a task data matrix D = [D ij ] M0×M0 , where D ij represents the size of data transmitted from task u i to its successor u j after the execution of u i .

3) Edge Server Model: When a ready task u i (i.e., a task for which all predecessor tasks have been executed) arrives at an edge server, the system provides virtual machines to perform u i . We consider that edge servers operate in discrete states, where each state corresponds to a specific voltage level and frequency level of CPU [15]. DVFS technology is employed to adjust the machine's operational state according to the CPU's workload, thereby optimizing the energy consumption. We consider each edge server has L discrete Voltage/Frequency (V/F) levels {(v 1 , f 1 ), . . . , (v L , f L )}, and use the following power consumption model [16], where the power of θ k working at the

L g is the number of logic gates, K 1 , K 2 and K 3 are parameters related to the type of processor, v b is the reverse bias voltage, I b is the junction leakage current, and C e is the average switching capacitance. We consider task-level DVFS, and thus, if task u i is assigned to edge server S k and is executed with the V/F level (v l , f l ), the computation time and energy of u i are given by t comp i = C i /f l and e comp i = P l t comp i , respectively. 4) Communication Link Model: In a typical edge network, the communication links are divided into the edge links E E directly connecting to the edge servers and the core links E B in the switching network. Therefore, we derive a matrix A = [a kn ] K×N to describe the state of the edge link, where a kn = 1 denotes there is a link e kn between the edge server S k and the switch R n , and thus, S k can send the information to or collect the information in the switching network through R n . Additionally, a kn = 0 denotes there is no link between S k and R n , and a kn = -1 denotes link e kn has experienced a permanent failure. To simplify the problem, permanent failures of the edge server or switch can be treated as permanent failures of the communication links between them. As shown in Fig. 2(b), a permanent failure of the edge server S 4 at time t is equivalent to a permanent failure of link e 43 , and thus, we have a 43 = -1. Consequently, the state of the edge link is transited from its initial state A (0) to the current state A (t) :

Similarly, we obtain a matrix B = [b mn ]N × N to describe the state of core links, where b mn = 1 indicates the existence of a link ϵ mn connecting switch R m and R n , b mn = 0 indicates ϵ mn does not exist, and b mn = -1 denotes a permanent failure in the link ϵ mn .
5) Task Reliability Model: When task u i is assigned to the edge server S k and executed with the V/F level (v l , f l ),

div.p: , where η is the maximum error-tolerant rate, d f is the sensitivity of the failure rate corresponding to the frequency scaling, and f max and f min are the highest and lowest frequencies of the processor, respectively. If the reliability of task u i is lower than the reliability threshold R th , we perform task duplication to improve the reliability of the task, and each task can be replicated at most Ω -1 times. For instance, in Fig. 3, the original task set contains M 0 tasks, i.e., tasks u a , u b , and u c . Tasks u b + M 0 and u b + 2M 0 are the duplications of u b , while u c + M 0 is the duplicated task of u c . If the reliability of u b , u b + M 0 and u b + 2M 0 are both 0.9, the reliability of u b with task duplication is 1-(1-0.9) 3 = 0.999, and thus the reliability of u b is improved.

div.head: B. Problem Formulation
div.p: The problem under study is task mapping in multi-service edge networks to minimize the system's energy consumption under real-time and task reliability constraints. Therefore, we determine the following decisions: communication link selection, task duplication, task frequency assignment, task allocation, and task scheduling. According to task duplication, the maximum total number of a task u i and its duplicated copies are Ω. Thus, the total number of original and duplicated tasks is M = ΩM 0 , where M 0 is the number of tasks in the original task set U 0 . The dependencies among the total tasks are represented by a DAG G = (U , E), where the vertexes U = {u 1 , . . . , u M } represent the tasks to be executed, while the edges E represent the data dependencies between the tasks.

To formulate the target task mapping problem, we introduce the following binary and continuous variables: 1) If task u i is assigned to the edge server S k , x ik = 1, otherwise, x ik = 0; 2) if task u i exists, h i = 1, otherwise, h i = 0; 3) if task u i is executed with the V/F level (v l , f l ), y il = 1, otherwise, y il = 0; 4) ∀ε i ∈ E, if the communication between task u i and task u j passes through the core link ϵ mn , z ijmn = 1, otherwise, z ijmn = 0; 5) if tasks u i and u j are independent and they are allocated to the same edge server, and u i is executed before u j , λ ij = 1, otherwise, λ ij = 0; 6) the continuous variable t s i denotes the time when task u i starts its execution; 7) ∀ε i ∈ E, the continuous variable t cs ij denotes the starting time of communication between u i and u j . For the sake of problem formulation, let 1) N = {1, . . . , N }; 2) M 0 = {1, . . . , M 0 }; 3) M = {1, . . . , M }; 4) K = {1, . . . , K}; 5) L = {1, . . . , L}; 5) W = {1, . . . , Ω}. div.head: C. Problem Linearization
div.p: Since there exist nonlinear items such as h i h j x ik , h i h j z ijmn in (13), P1 is a MINLP, which is difficult to solve directly as it is N P-hard [17]. To solve this problem optimally, we transform it into an MILP by adding auxiliary variables and additional constraints. The details of the linearization method are as follows.

1) The nonlinear item caused by if-else comparison: Lemma 2.1: Assume that b is a binary variable while x is a variable within the 0 ≤ x ≤ s range. The following comparative relationship: x ≥ c ⇒ b = 0, and x < c ⇒ b = 1 can be described by a linear constraint x-(c-δ) s ≤ 1 -b ≤ x c regarding x and b, where c ≤ 1 is a constant and δ is a sufficiently small positive number.

According to Lemma 2.2, to deal with the nonlinear item x ik y il in (12) as an example, we introduce a binary variable θ il = h i y il , and thus, the nonlinear item x ik y il can be reformulated linearly as follows:

div.head: III. EXPERIMENTAL RESULT
div.p: In this section, we perform a wide range of experiments based on simulation to evaluate the performance and effectiveness of the proposed task mapping and offloading algorithms. The simulation is carried out on a computer with an Intel i7 processor operating at 3.40 GHz and 16 GB RAM. The algorithms are implemented through MATLAB R2020a and Gurobi 9.5.1. The characteristics regarding the multicore platform and the dependent task set are summarized in Table I. We consider a multi-server edge system as shown in Fig. 1 with edge servers number K = 5, switches number N = 4, and the number In Fig. 5, we compare reliability and system energy consumption E T OT AL under different task mapping schemes: RATM with communication link selection and single path routing (SP) [8], where SP refers to data can only be transmitted over fixed core links between any two switches. In Fig. 5(a), we examine the impact of varying fault occurrences number N F (in routers, edge servers, or links) in the edge network on task reliability. We randomly generate 20 fault scenarios and task DAGs for each group and enforce i∈M x ik ≤ M 0 (∀k ∈ K) to prevent all tasks from being executed on a single server. The ratio of successfully scheduled tasks across all groups is denoted as ρ. The results show that RATM consistently achieves a higher ρ than the SP approach under different N F . RATM can dynamically select alternative fault-free communication links for data communication when a link fails, making it more resilient to permanent faults in the edge network. In Fig. 5(b), the results indicate that RATM achieves lower energy consumption than SP. This is attributed to RATM having a higher dimensionality of optimization variables, enabling it to select more energy- efficient communication links for task execution. Fig. 6(a) compares the change of system energy consumption E T OT AL under different task mapping strategies: our proposed RATM method combining task duplication with DVFS, task mapping only with DVFS (DVFS) [10] and only with task duplication (TD) [12]. The results show that RATM achieves an average 12.06% reduction in energy consumption compared to DVFS and an average 10.28% reduction compared to TD. To satisfy the task reliability constraint, DVFS uses a higher V/F level to execute the tasks, which leads to higher computing energy E CP . While task duplication alone can also meet reliability constraints, it increases the number of tasks, thus raising both the computing energy E CP and communication energy E CM . Combining task duplication with the DVFS approach minimizes task redundancy, enabling reduced energy consumption while still satisfying reliability constraints. the edge network is much higher than computing energy (i.e., γ > 1), tasks tend to be assigned to a single server to minimize communication energy, which increases M max and drives ∆ closer to 1. As γ decreases, tasks tend to be assigned to different servers to leverage parallel execution and reduce completion time, which drives ∆ closer to 0. Consequently, the energy consumption associated with communication and computation in the edge network is critical in determining task allocation strategies.

In Fig. 7, we compare the solution of problem P1 with the different objective functions, i.e., minimizing the energy (ME), minimizing the task completion time (MT), and balancing the energy and time (BE). The objective function in BE is:
div.formula: min µ E T OT AL E max + (1 -µ) t E M t max
div.p: , where E max and t max are the theoretical maximum values of E T OT AL and t E M , respectively. Results demonstrate that ME yields the lowest energy consumption E T OT AL , MT achieves the shortest completion time t E M , and BE provides an intermediate trade-off. Under ME, tasks tend to be allocated on fewer edge servers to reduce communication energy, increasing queuing delays and leading to longer completion times. Under MT, tasks are distributed across servers to enable parallel execution, which reduces completion time but increases communication energy. BE effectively balances energy and time trade-offs. In practical applications, the weighting coefficient µ can be adjusted based on specific requirements for real-time performance and energy efficiency to achieve the desired outcome.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSION
div.p: This study deals with the task allocation and scheduling problem in multi-server edge networks under multiple constraints. The edge servers are organized in a mesh network, where servers, switches, and communication links may experience permanent failures. To meet task reliability requirements, we propose a RATM method to allocate tasks to different servers and select appropriate communication links while optimizing the computing and communication costs of the edge servers. To mitigate the impact of transient faults during task execution and reduce the computing and communication overhead caused by task redundancy, we integrate DVFS and partial task duplication strategies. The joint design problem is formulated as a MINLP problem and then equivalently transformed into a MILP problem to obtain the optimal solution. Simulation results demonstrate that since task duplication, DVFS, and multipath communication link selection are jointly optimized, the proposed method outperforms other existing methods in terms of energy efficiency and task reliability.
